title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
Contents

The business question & dataset
How losses are distributed
Do vehicle types differ?
Are categorical factors material?
Correlations among risk factors
Fair comparison: the funnel plot
What really drives a claim?
Key findings & implications


This executive summary investigates what drives the profitability and volatility of a Spanish motor insurance portfolio. The analysis moves from describing how losses are distributed, through statistically testing candidate factors, to a multivariable model and a fair-comparison funnel plot, ending with concrete underwriting implications.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
The Business Question



“Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility are unknown.”

This study interrogates a real-world Spanish motor insurance portfolio to find those root causes — and to prove them statistically, not by intuition.


105,555


policy-year records · 30 variables · Spain, 2015–2018



No ready-made profitability field → I derive the Loss Ratio (claims ÷ premium)
Above 100% = a technical loss
Goal: validate drivers of profitability & volatility



The portfolio contains over 100,000 policy-year records across 30 variables. Because the dataset has no ready-made profitability field, the central metric — the Loss Ratio, claims divided by premium — is derived during data preparation. A value above 100% indicates a technical loss. All subsequent analysis revolves around explaining this measure.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
How Losses Are Distributed













How to read it
Each bar = policies at that loss level. The dashed line is break-even — left of it, the policy made money; right of it, claims beat premium.
The bulk sits left of break-even, but a long right tail keeps going well past 300%.



81% of policies never claim · among claimers, most stay below break-even · a heavy tail runs at a technical loss → profitability lives in the tail, not the average


About 81% of policies have no claim at all. Among those that do claim, the Loss Ratio is strongly right-skewed: the bulk of claiming policies sit below the 100% break-even line, meaning their claims cost less than the premium collected. But a long right tail extends far beyond break-even — I’ve capped the axis at 300% here so the main distribution stays readable, but in the raw data the tail runs much further, up to catastrophic policies whose losses exceed eight times the premium. The key insight for underwriting is that aggregate profitability is driven by this small, extreme tail rather than by the typical policy. This argues for tail-focused risk segmentation rather than across-the-board rate increases.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
Do Vehicle Types Differ?













All four vehicle types share a similar peak near Loss Ratio = 0
Motorbikes & vans show heavier right tails than agricultural
Quartile colours show wide spread (Q4 reaches the cap)
Shapes look distinct — but is the difference statistically real?



The ridgeline plot compares Loss Ratio distributions across the four vehicle types, with fill encoding quartiles. Motorbikes and vans show heavier right tails than agricultural vehicles. These shapes look visually distinct — but as the next slide shows, that visual difference does not survive a formal statistical test.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
A Formal Test Says: No













p = 0.32


Kruskal-Wallis · not significant


The ridgelines looked different — but the medians barely move: 0.60 · 0.64 · 0.76.
Vehicle type does not drive claim severity.

So the structure must lie in frequency — who files a claim, not how much.



A Kruskal-Wallis test returns p = 0.32, well above 0.05. Despite the visually distinct ridgeline shapes, vehicle type does not significantly affect claim severity once a claim has occurred. This negative result is important: it redirects the search for drivers away from severity towards claim frequency. Honest reporting of a non-significant result reflects sound statistical practice.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
The Large-Sample Trap



Statistically significant
χ² = 86.4, p = 1.5e-20
A textbook “highly significant” result.


Practically negligible
Cramer’s V = 0.03 · gap is only 18% vs 20%
The association is essentially zero.


Why? Sample size.
With 105,555 rows, even trivial gaps cross the significance line.
→ Effect size matters, not just the p-value.



The chi-square test is highly significant, suggesting area matters. But the effect size, Cramer’s V, is only 0.03 — negligible. The actual gap is just 18% rural versus 20% urban. With over 100,000 records, even a trivial difference becomes statistically significant. Reading the p-value alone would mislead; the effect size shows area is not a material driver.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
No Strong Numeric Predictor













Vehicle attributes are highly intercorrelated: Value–Weight 0.87, Cylinder–Value 0.79
Claim cost correlates weakly with all factors (|ρ| ≤ 0.09)
Premium tracks vehicle attributes (0.39–0.44), not actual loss
No single variable predicts loss → risk is idiosyncratic



The heatmap shows two things. Vehicle attributes are highly intercorrelated — value, weight, power and cylinder capacity all measure the same underlying size. More importantly, claim cost correlates only weakly with every factor. No single numeric variable predicts loss; risk in this portfolio is largely idiosyncratic, which is why a multivariable approach is needed.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
section: A Fair Comparison: The Funnel Plot
text:
A Fair Comparison: The Funnel Plot











A funnel plot object with 8 points of which 2 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 




Inside the funnel → noise
Small segments (agricultural, ~850 policies) swing by chance and sit deep inside the limits. The largest segment (cars, ~60,000) lands on the mean line — stable.


Outside the limits → real
2 of 8 segments fall outside the control limits — genuinely unusual, not sampling noise. Limits are adjusted for overdispersion, so the test is fair across segment sizes.



The funnel plot reframes the comparison correctly. The two agricultural segments sit far left with very low exposure — a naive ranking would call them the safest, but their position inside the wide funnel shows this is noise, not signal. Two segments fall outside the control limits and are genuinely high-risk. The largest segment lies on the mean line, confirming stability. The plot adjusts for overdispersion, appropriate for insurance claims.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
What Really Drives a Claim?













Vehicle type is the one robust driver of claim incidence
Vans & cars have OR < 1 → lower odds than motorbikes
Numeric factors (age, value, power) cluster at OR ≈ 1 → little effect
Agricultural OR ≈ 100 but CI > 1,000 → small-sample noise
Funnel plot & model cross-validate each other



The forest plot delivers the clearest answer. After controlling for all factors, vehicle type is the one robust driver: vans and passenger cars have significantly lower claim odds than motorbikes. Numeric factors cluster around an odds ratio of one. Agricultural vehicles show a huge odds ratio but an extremely wide confidence interval — an unreliable small-sample estimate, exactly the artefact the funnel plot warned against. The two methods cross-validate each other.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
Key Findings and Implications



What we found


Profitability is concentrated — about 91% of policies are individually profitable, yet a small catastrophic tail (Technical Result down to −€260,000) dominates the portfolio’s economics. Managing the tail matters far more than average pricing.


No single factor predicts loss — vehicle type (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.32), area (Cramer’s V = 0.03) and vehicle value (Spearman ρ = 0.13) are all statistically weak or negligible. Loss is largely idiosyncratic, not explained by the rating factors on file.


Structure lies in frequency, not severity — after controlling for all factors, vehicle type is the one robust driver of whether a claim occurs (vans & cars OR < 1). The dramatic “agricultural risk” (OR ≈ 100) was small-sample noise — confirmed by the funnel plot.



What to do


1 · Manage the tail, not the average
Focus underwriting and reinsurance on the rare catastrophic policies that drive losses, rather than raising rates across the whole book.


2 · Compare segments by exposure
Judge segment risk on a funnel plot that widens for small samples — not on raw claim rates, which made tiny agricultural cohorts look falsely extreme.


3 · Enrich the data
Existing rating factors miss true risk. Invest in richer features — driver behaviour, telematics, history — to capture the idiosyncratic variation current fields cannot.

section: 5.2 Distribution of the Loss Ratio (claiming policies)
text:
5.2 Distribution of the Loss Ratio (claiming policies)
Among policies that incur a claim, the histogram below shows the Loss Ratio is still right-skewed: many claiming policies stay well below the 100% break-even line, but a substantial group exceeds it and runs at a technical loss.


Code
sandbox %>%
  filter(Has_Claim == "Claim", !is.na(Loss_Ratio_capped)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Loss_Ratio_capped)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2c7fb8", colour = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "red", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.05, y = Inf, label = "Break-even (100%)", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, colour = "red", size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Among claiming policies, many run at a technical loss", subtitle = "Loss Ratio of policies with a claim (capped at 99th percentile)", x = "Loss Ratio (Claims / Premium)", y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









The distribution is strongly right-skewed. The majority of claiming policies sit below the 100% break-even line and remain profitable, but a long tail extends past it: a substantial share of claiming policies run at a technical loss. The spike at the 800% cap represents all policies whose true Loss Ratio exceeds eight times the premium — a small group of catastrophic claims that, despite their rarity, drive a disproportionate share of total losses. This confirms that profitability is shaped less by typical claims than by the behaviour of the tail.

title: Take-home_Ex01
section: 5.3 Loss Ratio by vehicle type — ridgeline plot
text:
5.3 Loss Ratio by vehicle type — ridgeline plot
Applying the ridgeline technique from Hands-on Exercise 4, I compare the Loss Ratio distribution across the four vehicle types. The fill colour encodes quartiles, so the central tendency and spread of each vehicle type are directly comparable.


Code
sandbox %>%
  filter(Has_Claim == "Claim", !is.na(Loss_Ratio_capped)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Loss_Ratio_capped, y = Type_risk, fill = factor(stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", calc_ecdf = TRUE, quantiles = 4, quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio distribution differs across vehicle types", x = "Loss Ratio (capped)", y = NULL) +
  theme_ridges()









The Kruskal-Wallis test returns p = 0.32, well above 0.05, so the differences in Loss Ratio across vehicle types are not statistically significant. The median Loss Ratios are also close (Motorbike 0.60, Van 0.64, Passenger car 0.76). This is an important negative result: although the ridgeline plot suggested visually distinct shapes, once a claim has occurred, the severity of that claim does not depend meaningfully on vehicle type. This redirects the search for drivers towards claim frequency rather than severity.

text:
6.1 Vehicle type vs Loss Ratio
Figures 2 and 3 hinted at visually different Loss Ratio shapes across vehicle types. Here I test whether this apparent difference is statistically real, using ggbetweenstats from Hands-on Exercise 4_2. Because Loss Ratio is heavily right-skewed and variances are unequal, I use a nonparametric (Kruskal-Wallis) test rather than ANOVA. To keep the plot readable on 100k+ rows, I work on a random sample of claiming policies.


Code
set.seed(1234)

br_dat <- sandbox %>%
  filter(Has_Claim == "Claim", !is.na(Loss_Ratio), Loss_Ratio < 5) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 3000)

ggbetweenstats(data = br_dat, x = Type_risk, y = Loss_Ratio, type = "nonparametric", xlab = "Vehicle type", ylab = "Loss Ratio", title = "Loss Ratio does NOT differ significantly across vehicle types")

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
6.2 Claim incidence vs circulation area
Since vehicle type did not affect the severity (Loss Ratio) of claims, I now turn to claim frequency. Using ggbarstats from Hands-on Exercise 4_2, I test whether the incidence of a claim is associated with the circulation area (urban vs rural) via a chi-square test of association.


Code
ggbarstats(data = sandbox, x = Has_Claim, y = Area, xlab = "Area", legend.title = "Claim status", title = "Claim incidence by circulation area")









The chi-square test is highly significant (p = 1.5e-20), which at first glance suggests area matters. However, the effect size tells a different story: Cramér’s V is only 0.03, indicating a negligible association. The actual difference is small — an 18% claim rate in rural areas versus 20% in urban areas. This is a classic large-sample effect: with over 100,000 records, even a trivial 2-percentage-point gap becomes statistically significant. Reading the p-value alone would overstate the importance of area; the effect size shows it is not a material driver of claim frequency.

Having found that categorical factors are not material drivers, I examine numerical risk factors. Using ggscatterstats from Hands-on Exercise 4_2, I test the relationship between vehicle value and claim cost (Spearman correlation, on claiming policies, sampled for readability).

  filter(Has_Claim == "Claim", Cost_claims_year < 20000, Value_vehicle < 60000) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 3000)

text:
6.4 Correlation among numeric risk factors
To see all numeric relationships at once, I compute a Spearman correlation matrix across the key numeric risk factors and visualise it as a heatmap with ggcorrplot. This also reveals multicollinearity (e.g. between power, cylinder capacity and vehicle value) that is relevant for later modelling.


Code
pacman::p_load(ggcorrplot)

num_vars <- sandbox %>%
  select(Premium, Cost_claims_year, Power, Cylinder_capacity, Value_vehicle, Weight, Age, Vehicle_Age) %>%
  drop_na()

corr_mat <- cor(num_vars, method = "spearman")

ggcorrplot(corr_mat, type = "lower", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 2.8, colors = c("#2166ac", "white", "#b2182b"), title = "Spearman correlation of numeric risk factors")









Two patterns stand out. First, the vehicle’s physical attributes are strongly intercorrelated — Value_vehicle and Weight (0.87), Cylinder_capacity and Value_vehicle (0.79), Power and Value_vehicle (0.76). This multicollinearity means these variables largely measure the same underlying “size and power” of the vehicle, and only a representative subset should enter any regression model. Second, and more importantly, Cost_claims_year correlates only weakly with every factor (all |ρ| ≤ 0.09): no single numeric variable predicts claim cost. By contrast, Premium correlates moderately with vehicle attributes (0.39–0.44), revealing that pricing is driven mainly by the vehicle’s physical characteristics rather than by variables linked to actual loss.

section: 7.1 Multivariable drivers of claim incidence — logistic regression
text:
7.1 Multivariable drivers of claim incidence — logistic regression
Univariate analyses found no single dominant driver. To assess each factor’s independent effect while controlling for the others, I fit a logistic regression for the probability of a claim. Because Figure 9 showed strong collinearity among vehicle physical attributes, I include only Value_vehicle and Power as their representatives. Coefficients are exponentiated to odds ratios and shown as a forest plot (broom + ggplot2).


Code
glm_dat <- sandbox %>%
  select(Has_Claim, Age, Vehicle_Age, Power, Value_vehicle, Type_risk, Area, Second_driver) %>%
  drop_na()

mod <- glm(Has_Claim ~ ., data = glm_dat, family = binomial)




Code
or_tbl <- tidy(mod, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)")

ggplot(or_tbl, aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = "#b2182b") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Which factors drive the odds of a claim?", subtitle = "Odds ratios from logistic regression (>1 raises claim risk); 95% CI", x = "Odds Ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









The forest plot delivers the study’s clearest answer. After controlling for all other factors, vehicle type is the one robust driver of claim incidence: vans and passenger cars have significantly lower odds of a claim than motorbikes (their points and confidence intervals sit clearly left of OR = 1). The numeric factors (Age, Value_vehicle, Power, Vehicle_Age) cluster tightly around OR = 1 with little independent effect. Agricultural vehicles show an enormous odds ratio (~100) but with an extremely wide confidence interval stretching beyond 1,000 — an unreliable estimate caused by the tiny sample, exactly the small-sample artefact the funnel plot warned against. The two methods cross-validate each other: what looked like extreme risk is in fact statistical noise.

title: Profitability & Volatility Drivers
text:
The portfolio’s fate is written in its tail and its claim frequency — not in any single rating factor.


Manage the tail · compare by exposure · enrich the data


The single most important takeaway: the portfolio’s profitability and volatility are driven by the catastrophic tail and by claim frequency, not by any individual rating factor examined. The three actions follow directly — manage tail policies, compare segments fairly by exposure, and enrich the data to capture true risk.
